The definition of a manifold in [Part 1 of General Relativity from Scratch](/explainers/gr-1-manifolds/) begins:
"a topological space that is Hausdorff and second countable, in which every point has an open neighbourhood
homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$". Almost every word in that sentence is topology. This explainer
builds the vocabulary from the start, with the manifold definition as the goal.

Topology studies the properties of a space that survive stretching and bending, but not tearing or gluing. It keeps
the idea of points being near each other, and throws away the idea of distance. A coffee cup and a doughnut are the
same to a topologist; a sphere and a doughnut are not.

## Open sets: nearness without distance

Start where distance exists. In $\mathbb{R}^n$, the **open ball** of radius $\varepsilon$ around a point $p$ is the set of
points closer than $\varepsilon$:

$$
B_\varepsilon(p) = \{\,q : |q - p| < \varepsilon\,\}.
$$

A set $U$ is **open** if every point of $U$ has some open ball around it that stays entirely inside $U$. Informally, an
open set has no edge: wherever you stand in it, you can move a little in any direction and still be inside.

![Left: the open disc. Every point, even one very close to the edge, has a small ball around it inside the disc, because the edge itself is not part of the set. Centre: the closed disc includes its edge, and no ball around an edge point fits inside, so it is not open. Right: sets can be neither open nor closed.](fig_open_closed.png)

Open sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ have three properties, each easy to check from the definition:

1. the empty set $\varnothing$ and the whole space are open;
2. any union of open sets, even infinitely many, is open;
3. the intersection of **finitely** many open sets is open.

The restriction to finite intersections matters. The intervals $(-1/n, 1/n)$ are all open, but their intersection, over
every $n$, is the single point $\{0\}$, which is not open: no ball around 0 fits inside a single point.

The insight of point-set topology, due largely to Felix Hausdorff in 1914, is that these three properties are all that is
needed. Nearness, convergence and continuity can all be defined from the open sets alone, without the distances that
were used to define them.

## The definition of a topology

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Definition

A **topology** on a set $X$ is a collection $\mathcal{T}$ of subsets of $X$, called the **open sets**, such that

1. $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $X \in \mathcal{T}$;
2. any union of sets in $\mathcal{T}$ is in $\mathcal{T}$;
3. any finite intersection of sets in $\mathcal{T}$ is in $\mathcal{T}$.

The pair $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is a **topological space**. A **neighbourhood** of a point $p$ is any set containing an open
set that contains $p$.
:::

The same set can carry many topologies. Two extremes exist on every set:

- the **discrete topology**, in which every subset is open. Every point is isolated from every other;
- the **indiscrete topology**, in which only $\varnothing$ and $X$ are open. No two points can be told apart.

On a set of three points, there are exactly 29 topologies (a brute-force count in
[`src/topology/count.py`](https://github.com/paulmilne/paulmilne.github.io/tree/main/src/topology) confirms the known
sequence 1, 4, 29, 355 for one to four points). Try building them:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
topoView = {
  const host = htl.html`<div></div>`;
  const mod = await import(new URL("topo.js", document.baseURI).href);
  mod.mountTopo(host);
  return host;
}
```

Finite topologies look strange, but they have a use: they are the natural setting for describing which states of a
system can be reached from which. Every topology on a finite set corresponds to a preorder on its points.

## Closed sets, closure and boundary

A set is **closed** if its complement is open. Taking complements turns the axioms round: arbitrary intersections and
finite unions of closed sets are closed.

"Closed" is not the opposite of "open". In $\mathbb{R}$, $[0, 1]$ is closed, $(0, 1)$ is open, $[0, 1)$ is neither, and
$\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are both.

For any set $A$:

- its **interior** is the largest open set inside it, the union of all open subsets of $A$;
- its **closure** $\bar A$ is the smallest closed set containing it, the intersection of all closed sets containing $A$;
- its **boundary** is the closure minus the interior.

A point $p$ is in the closure of $A$ exactly when every neighbourhood of $p$ meets $A$. This is "nearness" without
distance: $p$ is arbitrarily close to $A$ if no open set can separate them. Similarly, a sequence $x_n$ **converges** to
$p$ if every neighbourhood of $p$ contains all but finitely many of the $x_n$.

## Continuity

In analysis, $f$ is continuous at $p$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that points within
$\delta$ of $p$ are sent within $\varepsilon$ of $f(p)$. Topology replaces this with a statement about open sets.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Definition

A function $f: X \to Y$ between topological spaces is **continuous** if the preimage of every open set is open:
$$
V \text{ open in } Y \;\Longrightarrow\; f^{-1}(V) = \{x : f(x) \in V\} \text{ open in } X .
$$
:::

**For metric spaces, this is the same as the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition.** Suppose preimages of open sets are
open, and take $p$ and $\varepsilon$. The ball $B_\varepsilon(f(p))$ is open, so its preimage is an open set containing $p$,
so it contains some ball $B_\delta(p)$, and that $\delta$ works. Conversely, suppose $f$ is $\varepsilon$–$\delta$
continuous, $V$ is open, and $p \in f^{-1}(V)$. Some ball $B_\varepsilon(f(p))$ lies in $V$, and its $\delta$ gives a ball
$B_\delta(p)$ that $f$ maps into $V$, so $f^{-1}(V)$ contains a ball round each of its points: it is open. $\blacksquare$

It is preimages, not images, that behave: a continuous function can map an open set to a set that is not open. The
constant function sends all of $\mathbb{R}$ to a single point.

## Homeomorphism: when two spaces are the same

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Definition

A **homeomorphism** is a continuous bijection $f: X \to Y$ whose inverse is also continuous. If one exists, $X$ and $Y$
are **homeomorphic**: topologically, they are the same space.
:::

A homeomorphism matches open sets with open sets, so it preserves every property defined from them. Some results are
surprising at first:

![Left: the function tan(πx/2) is a homeomorphism from the open interval (−1, 1) to the whole real line. Length, boundedness and distance are not topological properties. Right: stereographic projection from the removed point N is a homeomorphism from a circle minus a point to the line. The same construction for the sphere gives the charts of Part 1.](fig_homeomorphisms.png)

The inverse must be checked separately. The map $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ from $[0, 2\pi)$ to the circle is a
continuous bijection, but its inverse jumps from near $2\pi$ to 0 as you cross the starting point, so it is not
continuous. A half-open interval and a circle are not homeomorphic.

This is the word in the manifold definition: a chart is a homeomorphism from an open set of the manifold to an open
subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. It is what guarantees that coordinates assign nearby numbers to nearby points, and vice versa.

## Making new spaces

**Subspaces.** A subset $A \subseteq X$ inherits the **subspace topology**: its open sets are the sets $U \cap A$ with $U$
open in $X$. The sphere gets its topology this way from $\mathbb{R}^3$, and a small open "cap" of the sphere, which is
the intersection of the sphere with an open ball, is open in the sphere though not in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Openness depends on
the space you are in.

**Products.** $X \times Y$ has the **product topology**, generated by products $U \times V$ of open sets. With it,
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\mathbb{R} \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}$, and a cylinder is a circle times a line.

**Quotients.** Gluing is the most powerful construction. Given a way of identifying some points of $X$ with others, the
**quotient topology** on the glued space declares a set open exactly when the set of all points glued into it was open in
$X$. Starting from a square:

![New spaces by gluing the edges of a square, arrows matching. One pair of edges gives a cylinder, or a Möbius strip if one edge is turned over. Two pairs give a torus, or a Klein bottle if one pair is turned over. Folding the edges in pairs from opposite corners, like closing an envelope, gives a sphere.](fig_gluing.png)

The Klein bottle cannot be built in three-dimensional space without passing through itself, yet as a topological space
it is perfectly well defined. This is one reason topology works with abstract spaces, not subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$. The
same freedom lets spacetime be a manifold that is not embedded in anything.

## The three conditions in the manifold definition

### Hausdorff

A space is **Hausdorff** if any two distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods. All metric spaces are: if $p$ and $q$
are distance $d$ apart, the balls of radius $d/2$ around them do not meet. Its most important consequence is that limits
are unique, since a sequence cannot eventually lie inside two disjoint sets at once.

Without it, strange things satisfy the rest of the manifold definition. Take two copies of the real line and glue them
together at every point except 0:

![The line with two origins. Away from zero it is an ordinary line; at zero there are two points, A and B. Each has neighbourhoods that look like an interval, so the space is locally like ℝ. But every neighbourhood of A meets every neighbourhood of B, so the sequence 1/n converges to both. The Hausdorff condition rules this out.](fig_two_origins.png)

In physics this would mean a world line that could end up at two different events, so the condition is assumed.

### Second countable

A space is **second countable** if its topology has a countable **base**: a countable collection of open sets such that
every open set is a union of some of them. For $\mathbb{R}^n$, balls with rational centres and rational radii form one.

The condition rules out manifolds that are "too big", such as the **long line**, made by gluing uncountably many
intervals end to end. The long line is locally like $\mathbb{R}$, and Hausdorff, but it is so long that no sequence can
reach its end. Second countability guarantees **partitions of unity**: families of smooth functions that let local
constructions, made chart by chart, be glued into global ones. That is how [Part 3](/explainers/gr-3-metric-and-spacetime/)
puts a Riemannian metric on any smooth manifold.

### Compactness

A space is **compact** if every covering of it by open sets has a finite subcovering. In $\mathbb{R}^n$, by the
**Heine–Borel theorem**, a set is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. The sphere, the torus and $[0, 1]$ are
compact. $\mathbb{R}$ and $(0, 1)$ are not: the open intervals $(1/n, 1)$ cover $(0, 1)$, and no finite number of them do.

Compactness survives continuous maps: **the continuous image of a compact space is compact**. If $f: X \to Y$ is continuous
and $\{V_i\}$ covers $f(X)$ by open sets, the preimages $f^{-1}(V_i)$ cover $X$. Finitely many of them do, so the
corresponding finitely many $V_i$ cover $f(X)$. $\blacksquare$

That one-line proof is the argument used in Part 1 to show that the sphere needs at least two charts. A single chart
would be a homeomorphism from the compact sphere onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$, which would then have to be
compact, and so closed and bounded. But the plane is connected (below), so the only non-empty subset of it that is both
open and closed is the whole plane, which is not bounded. So no such chart exists.

## Connectedness

A space is **connected** if it cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open sets. It is **path-connected** if any two
points can be joined by a continuous path. Path-connected spaces are connected; the converse fails for the
"topologist's sine curve", the graph of $\sin(1/x)$ for $x > 0$ together with the segment it oscillates towards at $x = 0$.
For manifolds the two notions coincide.

$\mathbb{R}$ is connected, which is the topological core of the intermediate value theorem: a continuous image of a
connected space is connected, so a continuous real function cannot jump over a value.

## Topological invariants

To prove two spaces are **not** homeomorphic, find a property that one has and the other lacks. Compactness distinguishes
the sphere from the plane. Connectedness distinguishes a line from a line with a point removed. Subtler invariants
distinguish the sphere from the torus.

The oldest is the **Euler characteristic**. Divide a surface into polygons with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces;
the number $\chi = V - E + F$ does not depend on how it is divided. For every convex polyhedron (all homeomorphic to a
sphere) $\chi = 2$: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron and icosahedron all give $4 - 6 + 4$, $8 - 12 + 6$, $6 - 12 + 8$ and
$12 - 30 + 20$. For a torus, divided into a 3 by 3 grid of squares, $\chi = 9 - 18 + 9 = 0$. So a sphere and a torus are
not homeomorphic.

The Euler characteristic also controls vector fields. The **Poincaré–Hopf theorem** says that on a compact surface the
zeros of any vector field, counted with signs, add up to $\chi$. On a sphere, $\chi = 2 \ne 0$, so every vector field has a
zero: you cannot comb a hairy ball flat. That is the reason, given in [Part 3](/explainers/gr-3-metric-and-spacetime/), that
a compact manifold carries a Lorentzian metric, the kind spacetime needs, only if its Euler characteristic is zero.

## Topology and spacetime

Einstein's equations are local: they relate curvature to matter at each point. They do not fix the global topology of
spacetime, which has to be chosen or inferred. Some examples from the series:

- **de Sitter space** ([Part 7](/explainers/gr-7-de-sitter-solved/)) has the topology $\mathbb{R} \times S^3$: a
  3-sphere of space at each moment of time. Its flat slicing covers a region with topology $\mathbb{R}^4$, which is why
  it can look like an ordinary expanding flat universe.
- **Anti-de Sitter space**, as a hyperboloid, has topology $S^1 \times \mathbb{R}^3$, with time running round a circle.
  The closed timelike curves this causes are removed by passing to the **universal cover**, which unwraps the circle into
  a line: a purely topological step.
- **Our universe** is consistent with flat space, but flat space need not be infinite: a flat 3-torus, made by gluing
  opposite faces of a cube, would look the same locally. Searches for repeated patterns in the cosmic microwave
  background have found none, which puts any such repetition scale beyond roughly the size of the observable universe.
- **Wormholes** change topology: a space with a wormhole is not homeomorphic to ordinary space, because a loop through the
  wormhole cannot be shrunk to a point.

## Summary

- A topology on a set is a collection of "open" sets closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections, and
  containing the empty set and the whole set.
- Continuity means preimages of open sets are open; for metric spaces it is the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition.
- A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. Homeomorphic spaces are topologically identical. A
  chart on a manifold is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
- Subspaces, products and quotients make new spaces. Gluing a square gives the cylinder, Möbius strip, torus, Klein
  bottle and sphere.
- The manifold definition needs Hausdorff (unique limits; no line with two origins) and second countable (no long line;
  partitions of unity exist).
- Compactness, connectedness and the Euler characteristic are invariants: they tell spaces apart, and they constrain
  what can live on them, including Lorentzian metrics.
